collection_summary:
Original `aggregation` instance filling one of the largest remaining gap-4 categories (aggregation: 1 reg + 0 staged → 1 staged). First **Technology/Programming** subdomain instance — Technology family extends from 1 (Inventions) to 2. Entity diversity: programming languages (NEW entity class) × decade partition. Natural human query phrasing: 'List the decades in which programming languages first appeared per Wikipedia's Timeline of programming languages, with the count, a representative example, and its designer.'

Multi-wiki source plan (15 URLs; cycle-1 unchanged): Wikipedia 'Timeline of programming languages' as the universe + count source; 13 per-language Wikipedia articles for Designer attributes (1790s and 1800s share the Jacquard_loom article); Year of First Appearance is sourced from Timeline article entries under the 'Timeline Entry Start Year' rule; Wikipedia 'List of programming languages' as cross-validation. Aggregation primitive is GROUP BY decade COUNT(language) — clean and source-recoverable. Result: 14 rows × 5 columns (Decade, Language Count, Representative Language, Primary Designer, Year of First Appearance) — cycle-1 audit replaced cycle-0 'Country of Origin' column with 'Year of First Appearance' to fix B3 source-grounding, single-key PK on Decade, 0 duplicates.

Universe covers all 14 decades represented in the Timeline article (decades with at least one entry): 1790s through 2020s, excluding 10 unrepresented decades (1810s, 1820s, 1850s, 1860s, 1880s, 1890s, 1900s, 1910s, 1920s, 1930s) — honest source-defined universe rather than padding with zero-count rows.

Cycles 1+2+3 + Fields-Medal-cycles lessons applied upfront: (a) explicit relation commitment to 'first-appearance year per Timeline article'; (b) deterministic decade boundary via floor(year/10); (c) Year of First Appearance is sourced from the Wikipedia 'Timeline of programming languages' article entry (cycle-3 commitment) under the 'Timeline Entry Start Year' rule for ranges (cycle-4 explicit; e.g., Plankalkül '1943-45/46' → 1943) — replaces cycle-0 'Country of Origin' which the audit flagged as not directly source-grounded; (d) honest universe = decades with at least one Timeline entry. Cycle-1 corrected counts per audit re-parse: 1940s 5→7, 1950s 46→48, 1960s 59→60; total 419→424.
source_coverage_notes:
Fifteen Wikipedia source URLs combine to support the aggregation. Decade-level Language Count derives from a single deterministic group-by over the Timeline article; per-row Representative Language is a curator pick (or the unique single entry for 1790s/1800s/1830s/1840s/1870s) documented in decision_log; Designer attribute derives from per-language Wikipedia article infoboxes; Year of First Appearance derives from the Wikipedia 'Timeline of programming languages' article entry under the 'Timeline Entry Start Year' rule (cycle-4 explicit for year-range entries like Plankalkül '1943-45/46' → 1943). Cycle-1 replaced cycle-0 Country of Origin column with Year of First Appearance to fix B3 source-grounding..

Roles:
- source_urls[0] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_programming_languages): universe + ranking + value (Language Count column). The article lists every notable programming-language entry with its year of first appearance, organized by decade. Per-decade raw entry counts (cycle-1 audit-corrected): 1790s=1, 1800s=1, 1830s=1, 1840s=1, 1870s=1, 1940s=7, 1950s=48, 1960s=60, 1970s=57, 1980s=68, 1990s=72, 2000s=54, 2010s=41, 2020s=12 (total 424 entries through staging-time 2024 cutoff). Cycle-0 had 419 from a pre-fetch summary that under-counted 1940s/1950s/1960s by 2/2/1 entries; cycle-1 audit re-parsed the article directly and corrected the counts. Counting rule: include every dated entry the Timeline article lists, including standard revisions and concept/implementation pairs — not curator-deduplicated.
- source_urls[1] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_programming_languages): validation. Alphabetical master list of every Wikipedia-articled programming language. Used to cross-validate that representative languages each have a dedicated Wikipedia article. Does not contribute to staged values directly.
- source_urls[2] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacquard_loom): entity-detail (1790s + 1800s representatives — both rows). Joseph Marie Jacquard developed the punched-card weaving loom in 1790s-1800s France; the article documents both the 1790 concept and 1801 implementation.
- source_urls[3] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytical_Engine): entity-detail (1830s representative). Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine design (1837 onward) — BAB L1 is the abstract notation Babbage developed for programming the Engine.
- source_urls[4] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Note_G): entity-detail (1840s representative). Ada Lovelace's 1843 note describing how the Analytical Engine could compute Bernoulli numbers — widely recognized as the first published computer algorithm.
- source_urls[5] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Begriffsschrift): entity-detail (1870s representative). Gottlob Frege's 1879 formal-logic notation — foundational for predicate logic and indirectly for computer science.
- source_urls[6] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plankalk%C3%BCl): entity-detail (1940s representative). Konrad Zuse's design of the first high-level programming language. Year of First Appearance: 1943 per Timeline article entry (cycle-3 audit fix; Plankalkül infobox states 1948 but cycle-3 commits to uniform Timeline Entry Year rule because pre-1950 historical entries — Jacquard loom, BAB L1, Note G, Begriffsschrift — have no software 'First appeared' infoboxes).
- source_urls[7] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortran): entity-detail (1950s representative). Verbatim infobox: 'Designed by: John Backus'; 'Developer: John Backus and IBM'; 'First appeared: 1957'. Cycle-5 audit fix: representative pinned to Timeline entry 'FORTRAN I' (1957 implementation, the first running version) — Timeline has multiple Fortran entries (concept 1954-55, I 1957, II 1958, IV 1962, 66 1966, 77 1977, 90 1990, 95, 2003, 2008, 2018, 2023). Pinning to FORTRAN I disambiguates the row. The Wikipedia Fortran article remains the source for Designer attribute.
- source_urls[8] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BASIC): entity-detail (1960s representative). Designers John G. Kemeny + Thomas E. Kurtz; Dartmouth College; first appeared May 1, 1964.
- source_urls[9] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(programming_language)): entity-detail (1970s representative). Designer: Dennis Ritchie; first appeared 1972 at Bell Labs.
- source_urls[10] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%2B%2B): entity-detail (1980s representative). Designer: Bjarne Stroustrup; first appeared at Bell Labs. Year of First Appearance: 1983 per Timeline (C++ infobox states 1985 — staged uses Timeline year per cycle-3+ rule; both place C++ in the 1980s decade).
- source_urls[11] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_(programming_language)): entity-detail (1990s representative). Designer: Guido van Rossum; Developer: Python Software Foundation; first appeared 20 February 1991. Year of First Appearance: 1991 per Python infobox.
- source_urls[12] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_Sharp_(programming_language)): entity-detail (2000s representative). Designer: Anders Hejlsberg (Microsoft); first appeared 2000.
- source_urls[13] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_(programming_language)): entity-detail (2010s representative). Timeline article entry: 2010. Rust infobox states 'First appeared: 2012-01-19' (first stable release). Cycle-3 staged value: 2010 per Timeline (cycle-3 audit fix from cycle-2's infobox-only rule). Both years place Rust in the 2010s decade.
- source_urls[14] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojo_(programming_language)): entity-detail (2020s representative). Designer: Chris Lattner; Developer: Modular Inc.; first appeared 2023. Year of First Appearance: 2023.

Validation note: every Language Count value is computed from a deterministic GROUP BY over the Timeline article — verifiable by re-counting entries per decade. Every Designer value is recoverable from the cited per-language Wikipedia article infobox. Every Year of First Appearance value is recoverable from the Wikipedia 'Timeline of programming languages' article entry (cycle-3 commits to uniform Timeline Entry Year rule — applies to all 14 rows including pre-1950 historical entries that have no software 'First appeared' infoboxes). Representative Language picks for the 8 multi-entry decades (1940s-2020s) are curator selections documented in decision_log; the auditor can challenge any pick. For the 5 single-entry decades (1790s/1800s/1830s/1840s/1870s), the representative is unambiguously the single Timeline entry — no curator judgment.

Universe-size sanity: 14 decades × 5 cols. Per-decade Language Count totals 1+1+1+1+1+7+48+60+57+68+72+54+41+12 = 424 (cycle-1 audit-corrected per direct re-parse of the master article). Decades not represented in the Timeline (1810s, 1820s, 1850s, 1860s, 1880s, 1890s, 1900s, 1910s, 1920s, 1930s) are excluded — the staged universe is honest source-defined.
decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with three documented risks. R1: counting rule must be deterministic — committed to 'raw entry count per decade in Timeline article' (no curator dedup of version revisions). R2: Representative Language is curator-judgment — the auditor can challenge the pick, but the per-language attributes (Designer, Year of First Appearance) are source-recoverable for any defensible pick. R3 (cycle-1 reframed): cycle-0 used 'Country of Origin' but the audit found country values not directly source-recoverable. Cycle-1 replaced the column with 'Year of First Appearance' (directly stated in per-language infoboxes). Cycle-2 further committed to infobox-only rule for Year (no Timeline-derived years). 14 rows × 5 cols comfortably clears the 10-row floor. Strong calibration gradient (LLMs know early decade reps trivially; 1990s/2000s have strong recognition; 2020s has very few entries so harder to predict count).
- Seed/provenance: ORIGINAL. No example_questions.txt seed addresses this exact shape; closest seed is #20 (decade × 5 inventions, scaled_enumeration) but the staged instance uses a different category (aggregation) and a different entity class (programming languages, not inventions).
- Category: aggregation — primary because the load-bearing primitive is GROUP BY decade COUNT(language). Secondary: multi_attribute_projection — because the table has 4 non-key attributes (Count + Representative + Designer + Year). aggregation has the largest gap among non-multi-source categories (gap 4 — 1 reg + 0 staged before this instance), making it the highest-leverage category fill among gap-4 candidates.
- Source plan: 15 Wikipedia URLs. Master Timeline article + List of programming languages cross-validation + 13 per-language articles for representative-language attributes (covering all 14 decades: Jacquard_loom shared by 1790s + 1800s rows). Roles documented in source_coverage_notes per the artifact-contract Source Roles convention. (Cycle-1 hygiene fix: cycle-0 had stale '10 URLs / 8 per-language articles' here from an early-draft 8-decade plan; the staged plan was 15/13 from cycle-0 finalization onward.)
- Expected shape: 14 rows × 5 cols, single-key PK on Decade.
- Domain: Technology/Programming — NEW subdomain (Technology family was previously only Inventions; this extends Technology to 2 instances).
- Risks/adaptation: per the three pre-gate risks above. Additional minor risks: (a) the Timeline article continues to evolve with new languages added each year — staged Language Count for 2020s reflects through-2024 entries only; (b) Wikipedia per-language article infoboxes (used for Designer attribute) occasionally get edited but are stable on the 5-year staging horizon. The Timeline article (used for Year and Language Count) similarly evolves slowly.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) First-appearance year relation: committed to 'Timeline Entry Start Year per the Wikipedia Timeline of programming languages article' as the load-bearing relation (cycle-4 explicit rule). The Timeline article tabulates a year (or year-range) for every entry; staged Year values use the start year of any range. Alternative relations (per-language infobox 'First appeared', designed-when, first-public-release) would yield different values for some languages (Plankalkül: Timeline 1943-45/46 → 1943 vs infobox 1948; Rust: Timeline 2010 vs infobox 2012; C++: Timeline 1983 vs infobox 1985) — the Timeline rule was chosen in cycle-3 because pre-1950 historical entries (Jacquard, Babbage, Lovelace, Frege) have no software 'First appeared' infoboxes, so Timeline is the only uniform source.
2) Counting rule: raw entry count per decade in the Timeline article, with NO curator deduplication of version revisions or concept/implementation pairs. The Timeline article presents FORTRAN I (1957) and FORTRAN II (1958) as separate dated entries; the staged Language Count counts them separately. Same for C90/C99/C11/C17/C23, C++03/11/14/17/20/23, Ada 80/83/95/2005/2012/2023, COBOL 1961/1968/1974/1985/2002/2014/2023, FORTRAN 66/77/90/95/2003/2008/2018/2023. An audit preferring 'distinct language family count' (which would dedup these) would yield a smaller universe (~150-200 vs 409) but require curator judgment on what constitutes a 'distinct family'. The Timeline-raw rule is honest and deterministic.
3) Decade boundary rule: floor(year/10)*10. A 1969 language is in 1960s; a 1970 language is in 1970s. No boundary-year edge cases. The Timeline article uses the same convention via its decade-organized section headers.
4) Representative Language picks (curator selection from each decade): 1950s=FORTRAN I (over Lisp/Cobol — most foundational, longest legacy in scientific computing; pinned to Timeline entry 'FORTRAN I' 1957 per cycle-5 audit fix to disambiguate from FORTRAN concept/II/IV/66/77/90/95/etc.); 1960s=BASIC (over Simula/ALGOL — most widely taught); 1970s=C (over Pascal/SQL/Smalltalk — most foundational, dominant systems language); 1980s=C++ (over Perl/Erlang/Common Lisp — broadest impact); 1990s=Python (over Java/JavaScript/Ruby/PHP — top single pick is hard, but Python edges in research+scripting+web breadth as of 2026); 2000s=C# (over Scala/Go — most widely deployed enterprise language born in this decade); 2010s=Rust (over Kotlin/TypeScript/Swift/Julia — most distinctive design philosophy); 2020s=Mojo (over Carbon — most associated with practical AI/ML applications). All 8 picks have dedicated Wikipedia articles with infobox-attested designers. Year of First Appearance values are sourced from the Wikipedia 'Timeline of programming languages' article entry (cycle-3+ Timeline-Entry-Start-Year rule). Per-language infoboxes are used for Designer attribute only.
5) [SUPERSEDED — cycle-0 only] Country of Origin column was replaced in cycle-1 with Year of First Appearance per audit B3 (country values not directly source-recoverable from cited per-language articles). The current schema has no Country column. Cycle-2 audit confirmed the schema rename; this item is preserved only as historical context.
6) Designer column: uses the Wikipedia per-language article infobox's 'Designer' field (or 'Designed by' equivalent). For multi-designer cases (BASIC: Kemeny + Kurtz), uses semicolon-separated form 'John G. Kemeny; Thomas E. Kurtz'. For C# the infobox includes the institution affiliation 'Anders Hejlsberg (Microsoft)' — staged value drops the parenthetical to keep the column to designer name only.
7) operation_type 'aggregation' chosen because the load-bearing primitive is COUNT GROUP BY decade. Secondary 'multi_attribute_projection' is captured in the secondary_category field.
8) Universe extension to 2020s: the staged 2020s row has only 12 entries (significantly fewer than other decades) because the staging cutoff is 2024 — the 2020s decade is incomplete. (Cycle-1 audit confirmed 2020s count of 12 unchanged.) This is honestly disclosed in temporal_note. A future refresh after 2030 would add ~30-40 more 2020s entries.
9) Cycles 1+2+3 + Fields-Medal-cycles lessons applied: (a) PK = Decade single key, no composite ambiguity; (b) per-row Wikipedia citation via Timeline article (count) + per-language article (Designer + Year of First Appearance); (c) explicit relation commitment in title and db_analog (Language Count: GROUP BY floor(year/10) over Timeline article; Year of First Appearance: Timeline Entry Year — uniform rule per cycle-3 audit fix, applies to all 14 rows including pre-1950 historical entries); (d) deterministic counting rule documented in source_coverage_notes.
10) Universe extension to pre-1950s: initial cycle-0 design covered only the 1950s-2020s decade range (8 rows) — below the protocol 10-row floor. Pre-cycle-0 fix: extended universe to include all 14 decades represented in the Timeline article (1790s through 2020s, with 1940s and pre-1940 entries from Jacquard, Babbage, Lovelace, Frege, Zuse). 5 single-entry pre-1950 decades plus 1940s (5 entries) plus 1950s-2020s (8 decades, 409 entries) = 14 rows total. The pre-1950 entries are well-known commonsense computer-science history (Lovelace/Note G is widely recognized as the first computer algorithm; Babbage's Analytical Engine, Jacquard's loom, Plankalkül, etc.) — strong LLM knowability.
11) Cycle-1 audit B1 (factual) — count corrections per direct re-parse of Timeline article: 1940s 5→7 (added Plankalkül publication and Short Code rows missed in cycle-0 fetch summary); 1950s 46→48 (audit caught 2 additional entries); 1960s 59→60 (1 additional entry). Total 419→424. Counts now match audit-confirmed direct article parse.
12) Cycle-1 audit B2 (structural) — db_analog rewritten as explicit two-step pipeline: (i) source-defined COUNT(*) GROUP BY floor(year/10) over Timeline article; (ii) curator_representatives_per_decade table for the curator-selected representative language; (iii) JOIN to per_language_wikipedia_article for designer + first-appearance-year attributes. Cycle-0 db_analog used FIRST_VALUE(language_name) which would have produced first-chronological representatives (Short Code for 1950s, ALGOL 60 for 1960s) rather than the staged curator picks (Fortran, BASIC). Cycle-1 db_analog now matches actual table construction logic.
13) Cycle-1 audit B3 (structural) — replaced 'Country of Origin' column with 'Year of First Appearance'. The cycle-0 Country column declared 'host-institution country' as the relation but the cited per-language Wikipedia articles directly stated only the institution name (IBM, Bell Labs, Microsoft, Mozilla, etc.) — not 'United States' as a country value. Recovering the country required following uncited institution-Wikipedia articles. Cycle-1 fix: replaced the column with Year of First Appearance. (Note: cycle-1 sourced Year from per-language infoboxes; cycle-3 later switched to Timeline Entry Year as the uniform rule because pre-1950 rows have no software infoboxes — see decision_log items 18-19 and audit_response cycle_3.) Schema column count unchanged at 5; column_types updated (categorical → numeric for the new column). Alternative would have been to add 6 institution-Wikipedia URLs (IBM, Dartmouth, Bell Labs, Microsoft, Mozilla, Modular) but Modular has no standalone Wikipedia article (Modular_AI redirects to Mojo), making the institution-URL path partially infeasible. Year-grounded approach is cleaner and more honestly source-defined. (Cycle-3 later switched the Year source from per-language infobox to Timeline article entry; cycle-4 added explicit 'Timeline Entry Start Year' range-scalarization rule.)
14) Cycle-1 audit HYG — fixed stale '10-URL/8-per-language-article' reference in the decision_log Source plan line (cycle-0 had this stale text from an early-draft 8-decade plan; the staged plan was 15/13 from cycle-0 finalization onward). Now reads '15 Wikipedia URLs / 13 per-language articles' matching the active source list.
15) Cycle-2 audit B1 (factual) — Year column mixed-source-rule fix: cycle-1 had Plankalkül 1943 and Rust 2010 (Timeline-derived) while all other Year values were infobox-derived. Cycle-2 audit flagged the inconsistent rule. Cycle-2 fix: committed to UNIFORM 'per-language infobox First appeared field' as the Year rule. Updated values: Plankalkül 1943 → 1948 (matching Plankalkül infobox), Rust 2010 → 2012 (matching Rust infobox 'First appeared: 2012-01-19'). Both decade attributions stable (1940s and 2010s respectively).
16) Cycle-2 audit B2 (structural) — db_analog alias mismatches: cycle-1 db_analog had counts CTE expose 'decade_start' but later projected 'c.decade'; representatives CTE exposed 'curator_selected_representative_language' but later projected 'r.representative'. Cycle-2 fix: aligned aliases — counts CTE now exposes 'decade' (not 'decade_start') matching c.decade reference; representatives CTE exposes 'representative' (not 'curator_selected_representative_language') matching r.representative reference. db_analog now self-consistent.
17) Cycle-2 audit HYG — scrubbed stale Country wording from active curation narrative: source_coverage_notes Validation note 'Designer + Country value is recoverable' → 'Designer + Year of First Appearance value is recoverable'; per-row Roles block entries that referenced 'Country: Netherlands' → 'Year of First Appearance: 1991'; decision_log items 4 (Designer/Country pair), 5 (Country of Origin rule — now [SUPERSEDED] historical marker), 6 (Country column captures institution), 9 (Country relation in cycles-lessons) all updated to remove active Country claims; collection_summary 'Designer + Country attributes' → 'Designer + Year of First Appearance attributes'.
18) Cycle-3 audit B1 (factual): cycle-2 committed to 'per-language infobox First appeared field' as the Year rule, but the audit caught that pre-1950 rows (Jacquard 1790s/1800s, Babbage 1830s, Lovelace 1840s, Frege 1870s) have no software-style 'First appeared' infoboxes — the Year values for those rows came from Timeline article entries / article body history. The cycle-2 'infobox-only' rule was therefore not actually uniform. Cycle-3 fix: switched to UNIFORM 'Timeline Entry Year' rule (the Timeline article tabulates a year for every entry, including pre-1950 historical entries). Plankalkül 1948→1943 (Timeline); Rust 2012→2010 (Timeline). All other Year values unchanged because their Timeline year coincides with their per-language infobox year. db_analog updated to reference Timeline Entry Year (t.timeline_entry_year) rather than per-language infobox (p.first_appearance_year). Both decade attributions stable (1940s, 2010s).
19) Cycle-4 audit B1 (factual range-scalarization): cycle-3 committed to 'Timeline Entry Year' rule but Plankalkül's Timeline entry is '1943-45/46' (a year range) and the staged scalar value 1943 had no documented scalarization rule. Cycle-4 fix: documented explicit 'Timeline Entry Start Year' rule — for Timeline entries showing a year range, the staged value is the start year of the range. Plankalkül '1943-45/46' → 1943 ✓. The rule applies uniformly: any future range entry would scalarize to its start year. db_analog updated to reference timeline_entry_start_year (was timeline_entry_year). Self-audit during cycle-4 also caught a C++ year mismatch under the Timeline-only rule: C++ Timeline entry is 1983, not 1985 (infobox value) — cycles 0-3 staged 1985. Cycle-4 corrected C++ 1985 → 1983. Decade attribution stable (1980s).
20) Cycle-4 audit HYG: scrubbed remaining 'per-language infobox' wording from active narrative where Year column was implied to come from infoboxes — collection_summary item (c) now says 'Year of First Appearance is sourced from the Wikipedia Timeline article entry'; collection_summary multi-wiki source plan now says '13 per-language Wikipedia articles for Designer attributes'; source_coverage_notes 'Designer + Year ... derive from per-language Wikipedia article infoboxes' → 'Designer ... from per-language infoboxes; Year ... from Timeline article entry'. C++ Roles entry 'first appeared 1985 at Bell Labs' → 'first appeared at Bell Labs. Year of First Appearance: 1983 per Timeline'.
21) Cycle-5 audit B1 (factual Fortran ambiguity): cycle-3+ committed to 'Timeline Entry Start Year' rule but the Representative Language column for 1950s used bare 'Fortran' which conflates multiple Timeline entries (FORTRAN concept 1954-55, FORTRAN I 1957, FORTRAN II 1958, FORTRAN IV 1962, FORTRAN 66, ..., FORTRAN 2023). Cycle-5 fix: pinned 1950s representative to Timeline entry 'FORTRAN I' (1957 implementation, first running version). Year 1957 unchanged. Decade attribution stable (1950s). Auditor's two-option proposal: 'use 1954 for broad Fortran' vs 'pin to FORTRAN I (implementation)'. Cycle-5 chose the pin-to-FORTRAN-I path because it is more rigorous (matches Timeline entry verbatim) and the 1957 implementation is the year most associated with 'Fortran' in pretraining corpora — minimizing LLM-knowability disruption.
normalization_decisions:
Decade values use compact form '1790s', '1800s', ..., '2020s' (English-language convention). Language Count is integer (raw entry count from Timeline article). Representative Language uses the Wikipedia 'Timeline of programming languages' article's exact entry name (cycle-5 audit fix: previously used Wikipedia article-title form, but languages with multiple Timeline entries — Fortran I/II/IV/66/77/90/95/2003/2008/2018/2023 — needed a pinned-entry rule). For decades with multi-entry counts, the representative is the most widely-discussed Timeline entry of its decade in pretraining corpora; for single-entry decades (1790s/1800s/1830s/1840s/1870s), the representative is the unique Timeline entry. The 1950s representative is 'FORTRAN I' (Timeline entry '1957 | FORTRAN I'), not bare 'Fortran' which would conflate multiple Timeline entries. Primary Designer uses Wikipedia infobox-attested name(s); for multi-designer cases (BASIC: Kemeny + Kurtz), uses semicolon-separated form 'John G. Kemeny; Thomas E. Kurtz'. Year of First Appearance is integer, sourced UNIFORMLY from the Wikipedia 'Timeline of programming languages' article entry under the **'Timeline Entry Start Year'** rule (cycle-4 explicit): for Timeline entries showing a year range (e.g., Plankalkül '1943-45/46', LISP concept '1956-58'), the staged scalar value is the start year of the range. Plankalkül 1943 (Timeline range start; was 1948 per infobox in cycle-2). Rust 2010 (Timeline; was 2012 per infobox in cycle-2). C++ 1983 (Timeline; cycles 0-3 had 1985 from infobox — cycle-4 corrected to align with Timeline-only rule). All other rows have Timeline Entry Year coincident with per-language infobox year. Decade attributions stable for all year corrections. Sort order is (Decade ASC) — chronological. The Timeline article uses the same chronological convention.

Counting rule (Language Count column): raw entry count per decade as the Timeline article presents them. Standard revisions (FORTRAN II/IV/66/77/90, COBOL 1961/1968/1974/1985/2002/2014/2023, C90/C99/C11/C17/C23, C++03/11/14/17/20/23, Ada 80/83/95/2005/2012/2023) are counted as separate entries. Concept/implementation pairs (LISP concept 1958 + LISP implementation 1959; etc.) are counted as separate entries. Per-decade staged Language Count (cycle-1 audit-corrected): 1790s=1, 1800s=1, 1830s=1, 1840s=1, 1870s=1, 1940s=7, 1950s=48, 1960s=60, 1970s=57, 1980s=68, 1990s=72, 2000s=54, 2010s=41, 2020s=12 (total 424; cycle-0 had 419 from a pre-fetch under-count corrected by audit re-parse).

Universe rule: include every decade in which the Timeline article has at least one entry. Decades with zero entries (1810s, 1820s, 1850s, 1860s, 1880s, 1890s, 1900s, 1910s, 1920s, 1930s) are excluded from the staged data — honest source-defined universe rather than padding with zero-count rows.

Representative Language: curator selection for the 8 multi-entry decades (1940s-2020s); unambiguous unique entry for the 5 single-entry decades (1790s/1800s/1830s/1840s/1870s). Documented in decision_log.
open_questions: 1) The Counting rule is 'raw entry count per Timeline article' which counts standard revisions and version pairs separately. An LLM under test might count distinct language families (~150-200 vs 409) — both readings are defensible; the staged data uses the source-defined raw count. 2) Representative Language picks are curator selections; an LLM under test naming alternative representative languages (e.g., Java for 1990s instead of Python; Go for 2000s instead of C#) is semantically defensible. The Designer and Year of First Appearance attributes would change accordingly. Cycle-5 audit pinned the 1950s representative to Timeline entry 'FORTRAN I' (vs bare 'Fortran') for disambiguation — Timeline has multiple Fortran entries. 3) (cycle-4 update) Year of First Appearance uniformly sourced from Wikipedia 'Timeline of programming languages' article entry under the 'Timeline Entry Start Year' rule (cycle-4 explicit for year-range entries). Plankalkül 1943 (range '1943-45/46' → start year), Rust 2010, C++ 1983 (all from Timeline; differ from per-language infoboxes 1948, 2012, 1985 respectively). 4) The 2020s row has only 12 entries because the staging cutoff is 2024 — the 2020s decade is structurally incomplete. A future refresh after 2030 would add 30-40 more entries. 5) Rust year discrepancy resolved (cycle-3): staged value is 2010 per Timeline article. Cycle-2 had used 2012 per infobox; cycle-3 audit found pre-1950 rows have no infoboxes so Timeline rule is the only uniform source. Both years place Rust in the 2010s decade. 6) An audit could prefer a different universe filter — e.g., 'languages with their own English Wikipedia article' (~500 languages) vs 'languages in the Timeline article' (~409 entries) vs 'TIOBE Top 50 popularity ranking' (~50 languages). The staged choice is the Timeline article — the broadest source-defined universe with stable decade-organized structure. 7) The aggregation primitive could be extended to include MIN/MAX year per decade (e.g., earliest entry in 1950s = 1950 Short Code; latest in 1950s = 1959 multiple) — kept out of the staged table for column-count simplicity (5 cols vs 7). 8) Future Wikipedia edits to the Timeline article could shift Language Count values; the staged values reflect the article state at access date 2026-04-30. 9) Universe extends from 1790s through 2020s (14 decades) — covers all decades the Timeline article has at least one entry. Decades with zero entries (1810s, 1820s, 1850s, 1860s, 1880s, 1890s, 1900s, 1910s, 1920s, 1930s) are excluded honestly. An audit preferring to include zero-count rows for completeness would yield 24 rows (every decade 1790-2020s); the staged choice is the source-defined positive-count universe.
